title: Beyond Silos: A state policy playbook for building integrated education-to-career systems
author: Michael B. Horn, Mallory Dwinal-Palisch, Angela Jackson, and Danny Curtis
summary: This is the framing paper of a six-part Clayton Christensen Institute series, syndicated on Michael Horn's Substack, on why career-connected learning keeps stalling at the pilot stage. The authors argue the education-to-career pipeline leaks at every joint and that the leaks are structural rather than accidental, because K-12, higher education and workforce development were each optimized for different missions and are now asked to mesh gears built to turn in different directions. They marshal a dense evidence base for the failure at every level of attainment, from collapsing high school wage premiums to the forty million Americans with some college and no credential to the finding that most of the 1.1 million nondegree credentials on offer deliver zero or negative value. The analytic engine is Christensen's Business Model Theory, which predicts that organizations absorb innovations fitting their value proposition, resources, processes and financial formula and quietly reshape the ones that do not. States are named as the level of government best positioned to rewrite those conditions, since they set authorization rules, funding streams and accountability systems. The paper pairs this with Chesterton's Fence as a discipline against demolition, insisting reformers understand why a barrier was built before clearing it.
points: The authors locate the binding constraint not in any single system's weakness but in the silos that stop K-12 reach, higher education depth and workforce labor-market focus from combining.
Business Model Theory is used predictively, to explain why schools and colleges adapt reforms to fit their existing design rather than redesigning around the reform.
Productivity losses from inefficient career transitions and related learning gaps are put at $1.1 trillion a year, close to five percent of US GDP.
Evidence on skill churn is used to argue urgency: one third of skills in the average job description turned over between 2021 and 2024, and twice as fast in the most AI-exposed jobs.
Chesterton's Fence functions as the series' guardrail, recasting reform as careful renovation rather than clearing away rules whose original purpose is not yet understood.
quotes: The American education-to-career pipeline is leaking at every joint. Too many learners are spilling out, lacking the knowledge, skills, experiences, or credentials needed to enjoy good careers.

Too few students participate in meaningful work experiences as part of their education, develop skills with labor-market value, or form clear pictures of the jobs for which they are preparing. The result? Learners struggle to turn education into opportunity, while employers grapple to find prepared workers.

Those solutions depend on the three primary systems that prepare people for careers: K–12, higher education, and workforce development. Each contributes important strengths. None on its own, however, can deliver the depth and scale of career readiness that today’s economy requires.

Without practical answers to these challenges, ambitious visions won’t become reality. This series of white papers is a guide for state officials and those who support and champion their work. It shows how to break down the silos between education and workforce systems and create the conditions for schools, colleges, and training providers to better prepare students for the workforce.

This mismatch is not just a hiring headache. It is a drag on growth. Productivity losses from inefficient career transitions and related learning gaps are estimated at $1.1 trillion annually—or nearly 5 percent of U.S. GDP.

Artificial intelligence is likely to intensify each of these challenges. As employers raise their expectations and skill demands continue to evolve, the goalposts are moving, and the bar is rising for learners before they even enter the game.

Each system, then, has its own limitations. K–12’s focus on college has pushed career readiness to the margins. Higher education’s prioritization of research and broad intellectual development has made it difficult to expand career-connected programs in high-demand fields. The workforce development system has struggled to steer learners toward high-value programs while expanding those that consistently produce strong career outcomes.
